sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *como si* from B2 Unit 15: it introduces a comparison with something unreal, and the verb that follows is always in the imperfect subjunctive (*Habla como si lo supiera todo*), whether the first verb is in the present or in the past. A campus that is also a gallery is full of such comparisons.

sections.title: Como si with the imperfect subjunctive
rows: Las nubes cuelgan del techo como si fueran nubes de verdad.
*como si fueran*: it is not true, it only looks like it
Los estudiantes caminan por el campus como si estuvieran en una ciudad.
El guía habla del arquitecto como si lo conociera.
*como si conociera*: he does not know him
Hablaba de arte como si fuera un experto.
after a past verb the rule is the same

items.spanish: Las Nubes de Calder cuelgan del techo como si fueran nubes de verdad.
items.english: Calder's Clouds hang from the ceiling as if they were real clouds.

items.spanish: Los estudiantes caminan por el campus como si estuvieran en una ciudad.
items.english: The students walk across the campus as if they were in a city.

items.spanish: El arquitecto diseñó el campus como si fuera una ciudad.
items.english: The architect designed the campus as if it were a city.

items.spanish: Habla de arte como si fuera un experto.
items.english: He talks about art as if he were an expert.

sections.content: After *como si* never use the indicative or the present subjunctive: *como si son* and *como si sean* are mistakes. The imperfect subjunctive marks the distance from reality, just as English says "as if it were".
